A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and are readable, including equations, figures and appendices. The original material in Appendices A–C can be matched, and v2's additional Appendices D–E are available for comparison.

before.justification: Section 6 and Figures 1–5 report original gridworld simulations comparing analytical and GDO representations while varying connectivity and representation dimension.

after.justification: V2 retains those simulations and adds original results for stochastic transitions and different goal locations in Appendix E, Table 1 and Figures 10–12.

M1.justification: The Laplacian definition, GDO objectives and weighted least-squares projection procedure are retained. The correction to Assumption 3.1 aligns its normalization with the already documented weighted objective; it does not establish an algorithm change.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates deterministic gridworlds with a bottom-right goal. V2 adds stochastic transitions involving random jumps and evaluates reward tasks with goals at all four corners and the center, substantially extending the tested environment conditions and task coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain analytical Laplacian eigenvector truncation and GDO-learned representations. The additional simulations use these same constructions; newly cited representation-learning methods are not added as evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: The original 15×15 grid, 1–50 walls, k=20 and Φ-norm evaluation protocol are retained. Added experiments introduce an η sweep from 0 to 0.9 and a 10×10 goal-location study with k=20; Appendix D uses 30×30 grids for connectivity visualizations.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained wall-count and representation-dimension analyses, Appendix E tests whether the connectivity–error relationship persists under stochastic transitions and different reward locations. Table 1 and Figures 10–12 provide substantial new sensitivity and robustness evidence.

E5.justification: Both versions report five-seed results and 10–90% bands. V2 additionally tabulates numerical ± quantities for GDO errors in Table 1, although it does not define the statistic represented by ±. No increase in the original experiment's run count is reported.

E6.justification: Figures 1–5 retain their original results. New Table 1 reports analytical errors of 0.172 and 0.00594, and GDO errors of 1.81 and 0.00876, at η=0 and η=0.9 respectively. Figures 11–12 add results across five goal locations. These are additional condition-specific findings, not performance improvements over v1 under matched settings.

T1.justification: Assumption 3.1 changes Euclidean orthonormality to Φ-weighted orthonormality. Appendix A adds a construction demonstrating nonunique optimal subspaces at a degenerate cutoff and Corollary A.1 with a proof argument for a bound using the preceding nonzero eigengap. The original main bound and other principal proofs remain.

C1.justification: Both versions claim a connectivity-dependent decomposition of approximation error, applicability without symmetric transitions, an equivalent Laplacian reformulation and gridworld validation. The revised wording and additional supporting material do not materially redefine these main contribution claims.

C2.justification: V2 explains how a zero cutoff eigengap produces nonunique optimal representations and relates λk and the cutoff gap to graph clustering. It also interprets the added simulations as extending the connectivity–error relationship. Existing limitations concerning GDO sample complexity and coefficient-estimation error remain.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-availability statement and repository address in Section 6. Appendix D also identifies NetworkX and spectral graph drawing as the tools used for the new visualizations. These disclosures are absent from v1.

R1.justification: V2 adds relevant citations, including Ahmed et al. (2025), Wang et al. (2022), Fouss et al. (2007) and Lee et al. (2014). It explicitly credits Section 4 as revisiting Wu et al., acknowledges related equivalence in Ahmed et al., and notes that Gomez et al. provide a correct general formulation in their appendix.

P1.justification: V2 locally rewrites the abstract, introduction, Laplacian discussion and conclusion, refines notation, expands Appendix A and adds Appendices D–E. The main section order and most existing prose and proofs are retained, so this is not a wholesale narrative reorganization.

P2.justification: V2 adds substantial visual material: four paired gridworld/transition-graph illustrations, three simulation plots and a numerical results table. Existing Figures 1–5 retain their displays but are redistributed across pages.

improvement.justification: The Φ-normalization correction improves consistency with the existing proofs, while targeted robustness results, clearer attribution and code-access information make the paper easier to assess. However, Corollary A.1 applies the main theorem to the first h learned features without establishing their required h-dimensional ε-optimality. This proof gap limits confidence in the new theoretical extension and tempers the overall improvement.
